doc.title: Kidd Jordan interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rome, New York, August 24, 2006

title: What to teach at jazz camps; Marlon's lesson
summary: Jordan wants technical work, playing by ear and unison writing; he refused to write Marlon a solo so he would learn to hear it.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: You tailored your own nickname. I’ll be darned. When you do these week long things at these jazz camps, if you had to prioritize what you want these students to go away with from it, is there a couple of things that you think are really important?

Well I like to do more than one week so we can get them on some technical things. Go through all the scales and show them how to go from minor scales and playing diminished and half diminished chords and all of that. And to check embouchures and fingerings and all of that. That sometimes I know the teachers tell them this, but when they come from somebody else then they’ll always listen. Oh yeah he said so and so and so and so. So I’d rather do that. And have them play something by ear, a lot of stuff by ear, just start making up little stuff, but just have some charts that, like we got, so that the ears is all filled and then we got something. And then let’s start giving them, I’d rather write in unison for them and let them start adding parts. See ‘cause that’s right. And like sometimes some of them discover that one of them was playing an alto part on a tenor. © Fillius Jazz Archive -21-

And I say all right now y’all got some harmony. And then they start switching off and doing the sections of the saxophone when we was playing. And I say, “don’t that sound good?” They say, “yeah it sounds good.” And I didn’t go through that with the trumpet section, but the saxophone section, even on “River Niger” they had their harmony going. And some other things. And I try not to do this. Just like that tune that you heard Kent spread out on [scats] “Mac the Knife.” You heard that chorale, that kind of thing? And I started that out with Kent and them. And Kent and them could hear all kinds of colors and all kinds of moving things. And I said, I listened to them and said, “yeah, that’s good.” So if I play I can play all of them. With me I don’t even worry about colors. Whatever I hear I’m going to do but if somebody puts the colors there then I’ll be able to flow through the colors. And I know how that works with them so other kids will come to me, “Daddy, show me this.” “I ain’t showing you nothing. Find out how to do it” and so and so and so. If you don’t do it — I remember Marlon, my younger son, “Daddy write this solo out.” He started crying when he was a little boy. “I want to play jazz.” I said, “no I ain’t going to write nothing out for you.” And he’d be sitting up there with the records and I’d run past the room and I’d play the lick. He said, “what?” I said I heard it. I don’t know what it is, I heard the lick. I played the lick. And after a while by the time he got in high school he could cop anything off a record. He could hear this and hear that. But I told him I said, “you see that?” You thought I was being really hard on you when you was a little boy, ‘cause he wanted to go to school and show off, I knew what he wanted to do. Said, “Daddy please” and went to crying and going on about it and my wife said, “well why don’t you write the solo out for him.” I said, “no, one of these days he’ll remember this and this will be the best lesson I can teach him.”
